```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"

knitr::knit_hooks$set(inline = function(x) {
  if (is.numeric(x)) x <- format(x, big.mark = ",")
```

Spectronaut reports every fragment it measured, including fragments with a
neutral loss and fragments that it excluded from quantification. The
hand-written converter removes the first and censors the second, by rules
that the columns of the export do not show, while a conversion specification
applies only the filters that it lists. This vignette shows the two rules, a
conversion specification without them, and what they change in the
differential abundance analysis. The conversion specification and the results
of the analysis were obtained once and saved, so the vignette runs without a
language model or the full export.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(MSstatsConvertLLM)
library(data.table)
```

# The export

We use the Spectronaut report of the three-species benchmark of Van Puyvelde
et al. (2022). Human proteins are present in the same amount in conditions A
and B, and yeast and *E. coli* proteins are not. We distribute the rows of the
first precursor in the report, one row for each fragment. The first
`r formals(infer_specification)$n_preview` are the rows the model was shown.

```{r export}
case <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "spectronaut_case_study.rds",
                            package = "MSstatsConvertLLM"))
rows <- case$rows
rows[, .(EG.PrecursorId, F.FrgIon, F.FrgLossType,
         F.ExcludedFromQuantification, F.PeakArea)]
```

# The rules of the hand-written converter

`SpectronauttoMSstatsFormat()` keeps only the fragments whose `F.FrgLossType`
is `noloss`, which removes the
`r rows[F.FrgLossType != "noloss", F.FrgIon]` fragment that lost
`r rows[F.FrgLossType != "noloss", F.FrgLossType]`. This is filtering. It also
sets the intensities of the fragments whose `F.ExcludedFromQuantification` is
`TRUE` to missing, which MSstats treats as censored. This is censoring, which
the converter's argument `excludedFromQuantificationFilter` turns on by
default.

```{r converter-default}
defaults <- formals(MSstatsConvert::SpectronauttoMSstatsFormat)
defaults$excludedFromQuantificationFilter
```

The rows come from a single run, so we keep the features with few
measurements. The censored fragments have no intensity left in that run, so
the converter drops them as well.

```{r hand}
hand <- MSstatsConvert::SpectronauttoMSstatsFormat(
  rows, removeFewMeasurements = FALSE, use_log_file = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
hand[, c("FragmentIon", "ProductCharge", "Intensity")]
```

# A conversion specification without them

A prompt that does not ask for filters returns a conversion specification
without them. We obtained the one below with llama3.1-8b and the
constrained_v3 prompt, in the benchmark of the manuscript.

```{r infer-live, eval = FALSE}
specification <- infer_specification(rows, "llama3.1-8b", "constrained_v3",
                                     acquisition = "DIA")
```

Here, we read the saved conversion specification instead. It has no filters.

```{r infer-saved}
specification <- case$specification
as.data.frame(specification$mappings)[, c("field", "from")]
NROW(specification$filters)
```

For some fields, it also reads a different column from the hand-written
converter, as listed below. So that only the filters differ, we set every
column to the one that the hand-written converter reads, which `GROUND_TRUTH`
lists first. This is the conversion specification behind the saved results
below.

```{r same-columns}
converter <- vapply(GROUND_TRUTH$spectronaut, `[`, "", 1)
fields <- specification$mappings$field
fields[specification$mappings$from != converter[fields]]
specification$mappings$from <- unname(converter[fields])
```

Converted by the LLM-based converter with this conversion specification, the
same rows keep every fragment. The excluded fragments keep their intensities,
and the two `r rows[F.FrgLossType != "noloss", F.FrgIon]` rows, with and
without the neutral loss, share the fragment name, so the converter takes them
as two measurements of one feature and keeps the larger.

```{r llm}
llm <- LLMtoMSstatsFormat(input = rows, llm_mapping = specification,
                          removeFewMeasurements = FALSE,
                          use_log_file = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)
llm[, c("FragmentIon", "ProductCharge", "Intensity")]
```

# Differential abundance results

We converted the full report with the hand-written converter and with this
conversion specification, and analyzed both with MSstats, as below. The
script `compare_puyvelde2022.R` in the GitHub repository of the package runs
these steps, with `REF_FILTERS=none`.

```{r analysis-live, eval = FALSE}
report <- fread("report_cut.tsv")
annotation <- fread("annot.csv")

converted <- list(
  hand = MSstatsConvert::SpectronauttoMSstatsFormat(report,
                                                    annotation = annotation),
  llm  = LLMtoMSstatsFormat(normalize_headers(report), annotation = annotation,
                            llm_mapping = specification))
processed <- lapply(converted, MSstats::dataProcess,
                    normalization = "equalizeMedians")
contrast <- matrix(c(1, -1), nrow = 1, dimnames = list("A-B", c("A", "B")))
compared <- lapply(processed, function(p) MSstats::groupComparison(contrast, p))
```

Here, we read the saved results instead. They have one row per protein. For
each converter, they give the adjusted p-value, `adjp_h` for the hand-written
converter and `adjp_l` for the LLM-based converter, and whether the protein
was called significant, `sig_h` and `sig_l`. `spiked` marks the yeast and
*E. coli* proteins, whose amount changes, and `in_h` and `in_l` say whether
each converter's results include the protein. A protein that MSstats could not
test, because one condition has no measurement, is never called significant,
whatever its adjusted p-value.

```{r results}
results <- case$results
head(results, 3)
```

The table below counts the proteins called significant by each converter, and
the yeast and *E. coli* proteins among them.

```{r counts}
counts <- results[, .(hand              = sum(sig_h, na.rm = TRUE),
                      hand_spiked       = sum(sig_h & spiked, na.rm = TRUE),
                      no_filters        = sum(sig_l, na.rm = TRUE),
                      no_filters_spiked = sum(sig_l & spiked, na.rm = TRUE)),
                  by = .(comparison = Label)]
counts
```

Without the two rules, the LLM-based converter calls `r sum(counts$no_filters)`
proteins significant, against `r sum(counts$hand)` with the hand-written
converter. The totals are close, but the two converters do not call the same
proteins. A call changed when one converter called the protein significant
and the other did not. We count it as near the threshold when the converter
that did not call the protein significant still gave it an adjusted p-value of
`NEAR` or less.

```{r changed}
NEAR <- 0.2
changed <- results[in_h & in_l][xor(sig_h %in% TRUE, sig_l %in% TRUE)]
near <- changed[pmax(adjp_h, adjp_l, na.rm = TRUE) <= NEAR]
c(changed = nrow(changed), near_threshold = nrow(near))
```

The two rules change the call of `r nrow(changed)` proteins, `r nrow(near)` of
them near the threshold.

# What to check

- Whether the hand-written converter of the tool, when there is one, removes
  or censors rows by rules that the columns do not show. For Spectronaut,
  these are the fragments with a neutral loss and the fragments excluded from
  quantification.
- Whether the conversion specification has a filter for each rule. Here, the
  filters keep the rows whose `F.FrgLossType` is `noloss` and the rows whose
  `F.ExcludedFromQuantification` is `FALSE`. A prompt that does not ask for
  filters returns none.
- After converting, `attr(converted, "diagnostics")` lists the filters that
  were applied and those that were skipped.
